analysis.one_liner: Ends the health insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 36 cosponsors from both parties, never received a vote — it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted insurance companies from the federal antitrust laws that forbid price fixing, bid rigging, and dividing up markets among competitors. This bill would strip that exemption for health and dental insurance specifically, so insurers could be prosecuted or sued for colluding on prices the way any other business can. The bill never moved past its first committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy health or dental insurance, if limiting anticompetitive conduct lowers premiums or improves the market; the Department of Justice and consumers, who gain the ability to challenge price fixing by insurers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that nothing in it 'modifies, impairs, or supersedes the operation of any of the antitrust laws with respect to the business of health insurance (including the business of dental insurance)' [S3].
It makes federal bans on unfair methods of competition apply to health insurance whether the insurer is for-profit or not, closing a loophole for nonprofit insurers [S2] [S3].

It keeps enforcement with federal and state law enforcement agencies and preserves private lawsuits by consumers harmed by unfair trade practices, so individuals as well as the Justice Department can act against collusion [S3].

The bill's own findings state the point plainly: Congress should not be 'playing favorites with certain industries or special interest groups by exempting one group from the general application of the law' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health and dental insurers, who would lose the legal shield that has protected them from federal antitrust suits since 1945; any insurers whose pricing practices relied on that shield could face lawsuits and enforcement actions.

drawbacks.text: The McCarran-Ferguson exemption does not block state regulation of insurance, and the bill would leave insurers subject to a second layer of federal antitrust enforcement on top of state oversight; opponents of similar repeals have long argued this duplication raises compliance costs that can be passed into premiums. The text itself notes state enforcement would continue alongside federal enforcement [S3].

Antitrust suits target collusion, not market concentration alone, so the bill would not by itself force competition in states where a few insurers already dominate; it changes the legal rules, not the market structure.

Health insurers have argued the industry is already regulated by states and by the Affordable Care Act's medical loss ratio rules, so the added exposure to antitrust liability would burden an industry that ordinary people ultimately pay for. This is the industry's standard objection to McCarran-Ferguson repeal and is not documented in the provided sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a straightforward fairness principle: one industry keeps a legal privilege every other business gave up long ago, and the bill would end it for health and dental insurance while leaving enforcement to the same agencies and courts that police everyone else. The main cost is potential litigation expense that could feed into premiums, and the remedy is limited — it combats collusive conduct, not existing market concentration — but the fairness case is strong and the mechanism simple.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred it to a subcommittee in February 2015, and no markup, vote, or further action ever happened before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gosar, a Republican, introduced the bill on January 22, 2015 [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day it was introduced [S5].
On February 19, 2015, the committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
It gathered 36 cosponsors, 33 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but no committee vote was ever scheduled and the Congress expired without the bill reaching the floor [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep their exemption from federal antitrust laws, because the bill died in committee without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keep their antitrust exemption

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican — 33 of 36 cosponsors — but it included 3 Democrats, and the bill was buried by a Republican-run committee rather than defeated by Democratic opposition.

industries.note: The bill would end their unique exemption from federal antitrust laws, exposing price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation to Justice Department enforcement and consumer lawsuits. The exemption's value comes at the expense of the people paying the premiums.
The bill explicitly includes dental insurance in the restored antitrust coverage, ending the same exemption for that market.
